issues: serving as the source of the river for this country → 為此國河源 = the source of the [Yellow] River of this country, i.e. China (Beal: source of the Yellow River); 從多河 is the Life's misprint for 徙多河
en_revised: The city leans against a steep ridge and has the Sītā River (從多河) to its north; this river flows east into the Salt Lake, runs underground, and emerges at Mount Jishi (積石山), and is the source of the [Yellow] River of this country (China).

issues: my wife and I → 與妻子 = with my wife and children
en_revised: Thereupon he set out, crossed the southern desert, and after six days arrived at the city of Baili (白力城) in the territory of Qočo (高昌). As the sun had already set, the Master wished to stop, but the city officials and the envoy said, "The royal city is nearby; please proceed." They changed to fine horses several times to press forward, leaving the red horse the Master had previously ridden for those following behind. He arrived at the royal city that very night at the time of cockcrow. The gatekeeper reported this to the king, and the king ordered the gates to be opened. When the Master entered the city, the king, accompanied by attendants carrying a line of candles before and behind, came out of the palace in person to welcome the Master into the rear courtyard, where he was seated within a precious curtained canopy in a multi-storied pavilion. The king paid his respects and inquired after him with great warmth, saying, "Ever since I heard of the Master’s name, I have been so joyful that I have forgotten to eat or sleep. Calculating the distance of the journey, I knew the Master would surely arrive tonight; therefore, my wife, my children and I have not slept, but have been reading the scriptures and waiting respectfully." Shortly thereafter, the queen and several dozen attendants also came to pay their respects. By this time, dawn was gradually approaching, and the Master said he was exhausted from the long conversation and wished to sleep; only then did the king return to his palace, leaving several eunuchs to attend to him overnight.

issues: who took both the people and their belongings and departed → 眾與物而去 = the party gave them goods and they went off (Beal: after giving them what they demanded, they departed)
en_revised: From here, traveling west, one arrives at the Father Teacher Spring (阿父師泉) in the country of Agni (阿耆尼國). The spring is located at a sandy cliff south of the road; the cliff is several *zhang* high, and water flows out from its midpoint. It is said in tradition that formerly there were several hundred merchants who, while on the road, ran out of water and, upon reaching this place, were so exhausted they did not know what to do. At that time, there was a monk among the group who carried no travel provisions and relied on the group to beg for his livelihood. The group discussed this, saying, "This monk serves the Buddha, which is why we have been supporting him; although we have traveled ten thousand *li*, he has brought nothing with him. Now that we are in such dire straits, he does not even show concern; we should go and speak to him." The monk said, "If you wish to obtain water, you should each worship the Buddha and receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts; I will then climb the cliff to produce water for you." As the group was in such a desperate state, they all followed his instructions. Once they had received the precepts, the monk taught them, "After I have ascended the cliff, you must call out, 'Father Teacher, bring down water for us,' and state however much you require." A short while after he left, the crowd made their request as instructed; in an instant, water flowed down in abundance, and everyone was filled with joy and gratitude. The master did not return, and when the crowd climbed up to look, he had already passed away (entered *parinirvāṇa*). Great and small, they wailed in grief and cremated him according to the customs of the Western Regions. At the place where he had sat, they gathered bricks and stones to build a stupa; the stupa still stands today, and the water has never ceased. For travelers coming and going, the flow is fine or coarse depending on the size of the group; when no one is there, it is merely a trickle. The Dharma Master and his group spent the night by the side of the spring. At daybreak, they continued on and passed the Silver Mountain. The mountain is very high and broad, consisting entirely of silver mines; it is the source from which the silver coinage of the Western Regions is produced. On the west side of the mountain, they again encountered a band of robbers; the party gave them goods, and they went away. They then proceeded to the riverbank where the royal city was located and stayed there for the night. At that time, several dozen Hu merchants who were their fellow travelers, eager to be the first to trade, set out secretly in the middle of the night; after traveling more than ten li, they encountered bandits who robbed and killed them, and not a single person escaped. By the time the Dharma Master and his group arrived, they saw the remains of the victims, with no property left, and were deeply saddened and lamented. Proceeding gradually, they saw the royal capital in the distance, and the King of Agni (阿耆尼國) came out with his ministers to welcome them and invite them in to receive offerings. As his country had previously been invaded and harassed by Qočo (高昌), the king bore a grudge and refused to provide horses. The Dharma Master stayed for one night and then moved on.

issues: Prajñāgupta (毱多) [twice] → 毱多 is Mokṣagupta 木叉毱多, the same man throughout (Beal: Mokshagupta); Moksagupta → Mokṣagupta
en_revised: After the meal, he went to the Ascarya Monastery (阿奢理兒寺) in the northwest of the city, which was the residence of Mokṣagupta (木叉毱多). Mokṣagupta was intellectually keen and agile, and he was the one whom the people of that land revered and followed. He had traveled and studied in India for more than twenty years; although he had engaged with many scriptures, he was most skilled in the *Śabdavidyā* (聲明), and the king and the people of the country all respected him, calling him peerless. Seeing the Master arrive, he treated him merely with the courtesy due to a guest, not yet acknowledging his mastery of the Dharma. He said to the Master, "In this land, we have the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* (雜心), the *Abhidharmakośa* (俱舍), the *Vibhāṣā* (毘婆沙), and all such works; studying these is sufficient, so there is no need to trouble yourself with the hardships of traveling to the West." The Master replied, "Do you have the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (瑜伽論) here?" Mokṣagupta said, "Why ask about that book of deviant views? A true disciple of the Buddha does not study it." The Master had initially respected him deeply, but upon hearing these words, he regarded him as no better than dirt. He replied, "The *Vibhāṣā* and *Kośa* are already available in my home country, but I regret that their principles are sparse and their language shallow, for they are not the ultimate teachings; that is why I have come specifically to study the Mahāyāna *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Furthermore, the *Yogācāra* was spoken by the Bodhisattva Maitreya, who is to be the next Buddha; if you now call it a book of deviant views, do you not fear falling into the bottomless pit of suffering?" The other replied, "You do not even understand the *Vibhāṣā* and the others; how can you say they are not profound?" The Master replied, "Do you understand them now, Master?" He said, "I understand them completely." The Master then quoted the opening passage of the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (俱舍) to question him, but he erred at the very beginning. As the Master pressed him further, his expression changed, and he said, "You should ask about other sections." The Master then presented another passage, which he also could not explain, saying, "The *Śāstra* does not contain these words." At that time, the king’s uncle, Jñānacandra (智月), who had entered the monkhood and was also well-versed in the sutras and commentaries, was sitting nearby and testified that the *Śāstra* did indeed contain those words. They then took the text and read it together; Mokṣagupta (毱多) was extremely ashamed and said, "I am old and forgetful." The Master then asked about other sections, but he had no good explanations for them either. At that time, because the snowy paths of the Ling Mountains (淩山) were not yet open, the Master could not proceed and remained there for over sixty days. Aside from sightseeing, he often went to converse with him; when they met, Mokṣagupta no longer sat cross-legged, but would instead stand up or move aside. He privately said to others, "This Chinese monk is not easy to contend with in debate. If he goes to India, even the most talented of the younger generation there may not surpass him." Such was his awe and admiration.

issues: those who froze to death → 𣨙凍死 = died of starvation and cold (gaiji 𣨙 read as 餒/殍 'starve'; Beal: starved and frozen to death)
en_revised: Traveling northwest for another three hundred li, he crossed a desert and reached the Ice Mountains (Língshān 凌山), which are the northern corner of the Pamir Range (Cōnglǐng 葱嶺). The mountains are precipitous and steep, reaching up to the heavens. Since the beginning of creation, ice and snow have gathered there, accumulating to form glaciers that do not melt in spring or summer. They are frozen, vast, and boundless, connecting with the clouds; looking up at them, they are dazzlingly white, and one cannot see their limits. Ice peaks that have collapsed and fallen by the side of the road are sometimes a hundred feet high or several dozen feet wide; because of this, the paths are rugged, and climbing is difficult and arduous. Furthermore, wind and snow fly together, and even wearing heavy furs and boots, one cannot avoid shivering from the cold. When wishing to sleep or eat, there is no dry place to stop; one can only hang a pot to cook and spread a mat upon the ice to sleep. After seven days, he finally emerged from the mountains. Among his companions, those who died of hunger and cold numbered three or four out of ten, and the losses of oxen and horses were even greater.

issues: Suyab (素葉水城) → the Life writes 素葉城 here; Its people are dark-skinned → 其人露黑 = the people go naked and are black (Beal: naked-blacks)
en_revised: Traveling over five hundred li northwest along the sea, he arrived at the city of Suyab (素葉城), where he encountered the Yabghu Khan (葉護可汗) of the Turks, who was then engaged in a hunting expedition with a magnificent display of horses and men. The Khan wore a robe of green damask, his hair was exposed, and he wore a band of silk about a zhang in length wrapped around his forehead, with the ends hanging down the back. More than two hundred high-ranking officials, all dressed in brocade robes with braided hair, surrounded him on the left and right. The rest of the military host were all dressed in furs and felt, carrying lances, banners, and bows, with cavalry on camels and horses extending as far as the eye could see, their numbers beyond reckoning. Upon meeting, the Khan was delighted and said, "I am going away for a short time; in two or three days I shall return. Master, please proceed to my headquarters." He ordered the high official Tamachi (答摩支) to escort and settle him. Three days after the Master arrived at the headquarters, the Khan returned and invited the Master to enter. The Khan resided in a large tent adorned with golden flowers, which were so brilliant they dazzled the eyes. The various high officials were seated in two long rows on mats in front, all resplendent in brocade garments, with the remaining guards standing behind. To look upon it, even for a ruler of a nomadic tent, it was truly magnificent. When the Master was thirty paces from the tent, the Khan came out to greet and bow to him; after exchanging greetings through an interpreter, they entered and sat down. The Turks worship fire and do not use beds, as they believe wood contains fire; thus, out of reverence, they do not sit on them, but merely spread double mats on the ground. Nevertheless, they set up an iron folding chair for the Master, spread a cushion upon it, and invited him to sit. In a moment, the envoys from the Han court and the country of Qočo (高昌) were ushered in to present their credentials and gifts; the Khan personally inspected them with great pleasure and bade the messengers be seated. He ordered wine to be served and music to be performed; the Khan drank with his ministers and the envoys, while grape juice was specially requested and offered to the Master. Thereupon, they toasted one another freely, with cups and bowls of various shapes being passed and drained in succession, while the clanging music of the frontier tribes rose in harmony; though these were melodies of barbarian custom, they were most pleasing to the eyes and ears and delightful to the heart. After a short while, more food arrived, consisting of the flesh of freshly slaughtered lambs and calves, which was piled up before them. Pure food was separately prepared and served to the Master, consisting of cakes, rice, butter, milk, rock sugar, honey, grapes, and so forth. Once the meal was finished, grape juice was served again, and the Khan requested a sermon. The Master then instructed him on the ten good deeds, the cherishing of living beings, and the practices of the pāramitās leading to liberation; the Khan raised his hands to his forehead, rejoicing and accepting the teaching with faith.  The Master remained there for several days, and the Khan urged him to stay, saying: "Master, there is no need to go to the country of Indu (印特伽國); that land is excessively hot, where the tenth month is like the fifth month here, and judging by your appearance, I fear you would melt away upon arriving there. Its people go naked and are black and lack dignity; they are not worth seeing." The Master replied: "I am going there now to trace the sacred sites and to seek the Dharma." The Khan then ordered a search throughout the army for someone who understood the Han language and the dialects of various countries, and found a young man who had spent several years in Chang'an and was proficient in the Han language. He was immediately appointed as a Madu (摩咄) official, tasked with drafting letters to various countries, and was ordered to escort the Master to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). He also bestowed a set of religious robes made of crimson damask and fifty bolts of silk, and together with his ministers, escorted him for more than ten li.

issues: Yexie River → 葉葉河 is Yeye (the Xiyu ji has 葉河), the Jaxartes
en_revised: The west of the country borders the Yeye River (葉葉河; the Jaxartes). Traveling west for over a thousand li, one reaches the country of Sutṛṣṇa (窣堵利瑟那國), which borders the Yeye River to its east. The river originates from the northern source of the Congling (Pamir) Mountains and flows toward the northwest.

issues: another Brahman monk → 一梵僧 = an Indian monk (Beal: a Brahman priest)
en_revised: From here, he traveled several hundred li and crossed the Oxus River (縛芻河) to reach the country of Huo (活國), which was the residence of Tardu Shad (呾度設), the eldest son of the Yehu Khan (葉護可汗) and the husband of the King of Gaochang’s younger sister. The King of Gaochang had sent a letter to his residence. By the time the Master arrived, the princess, the Khatun (可賀敦), had already died. Tardu Shad was also ill; upon hearing that the Master had come from Gaochang and having received the letter, he and his children wept uncontrollably. He then requested the Master, saying, "My disciple, seeing the Master, feels his eyes brighten; I wish for you to rest here for a while. Once I recover, I will personally escort the Master to the country of the Brahmins (婆羅門國)." At that time, an Indian monk (梵僧) also arrived and recited mantras for him, and his illness gradually began to subside. Later, he married a young Khatun who, having been instructed by his son from a previous marriage, used poison to kill her husband. After the Shad died, as the son of the Princess of Gaochang was still young, the Tegin (特勤)—the son of the former queen—usurped the position of Shad and took his stepmother as his wife. Because he encountered this funeral, the Master was delayed for more than a month. There was a śramaṇa there named Dharmasaṃgha (達摩僧伽) who had traveled to study in India and was regarded as a master of the Dharma west of the Pamir Range (葱嶺); none of the monks from Kashgar (疎勒) or Khotan (于闐) dared to engage in debate with him. The Master wished to know the depth of his learning and sent someone to ask the teacher how many sutras and śāstras he understood. His disciples were all angry when they heard this. Dharmasaṃgha laughed and said, "I understand them all; ask whatever you wish." The Master, knowing that he had not studied the Mahāyāna, questioned him on several topics from the Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra (婆沙) and other Hīnayāna teachings, which he did not understand well. He then apologized and submitted, and his disciples were all ashamed. From that time on, they met with joy, and he praised the Master everywhere, saying that he himself could not compare to him.

issues: Prakaraṇapāda (六足) → 六足 = the six pāda treatises of the Abhidharma, not one of them
en_revised: Upon arriving, he observed the city and its suburbs, which were spacious and open, with fertile plains and fields; it was truly a superior region. There were one hundred monasteries and over three thousand monks, all of whom were students of the Hīnayāna. To the southwest outside the city is the Nava-vihāra (納縛伽藍), which is adorned with great beauty. Inside the Buddha hall of the monastery is the Buddha’s washing basin, with a capacity of about one *dou*. There is also a tooth of the Buddha, one inch long and eight or nine *fen* wide, yellowish-white in color, which frequently emits a radiant light. There is also the Buddha’s sweeping broom, made of *kāśa* grass, over three feet long and about seven inches in circumference, with a handle decorated with various jewels. These three items are brought out on every fast day for the ordained and laity to view and pay homage to; those who are perfectly sincere are moved to witness the emission of divine light. To the north of the monastery is a stūpa over two hundred feet high. To the southwest of the monastery is a *vihāra* (精廬) that has been established for many years; those who have resided there to practice the path and attain the four fruits have appeared in every generation without interruption, and after their *nirvāṇa*, each has had a memorial tower, with their foundations connecting for several hundred. Fifty *li* to the northwest of the great city, one reaches the city of Trapuṣa (提謂城). Forty *li* to the north of that city is the city of Bhallika (波利城). In the city are two stūpas, three *zhang* high. Formerly, when the Buddha first attained the path, he accepted parched flour and honey from these two elders, who first heard the five precepts and the ten virtues and requested to make offerings. The Tathāgata then bestowed upon them his hair and nails, instructing them to build the stūpas and providing the ritual for their construction; the two elders took them back to their own country and built these sacred shrines, which are these very ones. Over seventy *li* to the west of the city is a stūpa more than two *zhang* high, which was built in the past during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha. In the Nava-saṃghārāma (納縛伽藍) there was a Hīnayāna Tripiṭaka master from the country of Takka (磔迦國) named Prajñākara. Having heard that the country of Bactria (縛喝國) possessed many sacred sites, he had come to pay his respects. He was intelligent and fond of learning, brilliant and spirited from his youth; he delved into the nine sections of the scriptures and immersed himself in the four Āgamas, and his reputation for doctrinal interpretation was known throughout India. He was thoroughly versed in the Hīnayāna *Abhidharma*, *Jñānaprasthāna* (迦延), *Kośa*, the six *pāda* treatises (六足), and *Abhidharma* treatises. Upon hearing that the Dharma Master had come from afar to seek the Dharma, they met with great joy. The Master presented his doubts and difficulties, questioning him on works such as the *Kośa* and the *Vibhāṣā*; his responses were extremely proficient and refined, so the Master stayed for over a month to study the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* under him. In the monastery, there were also two other Hīnayāna Tripiṭaka masters, Dharmapriya and Dharmakara, both of whom were highly esteemed by the local people. Seeing the Master’s brilliant and refined spirit, they held him in the highest reverence.

issues: Huimotuo (銳末陀) → 銳末陀 is Ruimotuo, Rūmīdh (cf. 01.33; Beal: Jui-mo-to); Guzganan → Gūzgān
en_revised: To the southwest of Balkh (縛喝) lay the kingdoms of Rūmīdh (銳末陀) and Gūzgān (胡寔健國). When their kings heard that the Dharma Master had come from a distant land, they all sent high-ranking ministers to pay their respects and invite him to visit their kingdoms to receive offerings, but he declined and did not go. The envoys came and went two or three times, until, having no other choice, he finally went. The kings were overjoyed and presented gold, jewels, food, and drink to the Dharma Master, but he accepted none of them and returned.

issues: Āryadeva (阿梨耶馱婆) → Āryadāsa (Beal: Aryadasa); the Prince of Song → 宋王 = Song Yu 宋玉, author of the Zhaohun lines quoted (Beal: Sung-yu); the level path lasts for only a few dozen feet → 平途數丈 ambiguous: DM kept; alternatively 'on the level the snow (Beal: mud) lies several zhang'
en_revised: Traveling southeast, he entered the Great Snow Mountains (大雪山), and after traveling more than six hundred li, he left the territory of Tukhara (覩貨羅) and entered the country of Bāmīyāna (梵衍那國). The kingdom is over two thousand li from east to west and is situated in the midst of the Snow Mountains. The roads are arduous and perilous, twice as difficult as those in the icy mountains and deserts; frozen clouds and flying snow never clear for a moment, and in the most extreme places, the level path lasts for only a few dozen feet. Thus, when Song Yu (宋王, i.e. 宋玉) spoke of the hardships of the West, with towering ice piled high and flying snow for a thousand li, he was referring to this. Alas, if one were not seeking the unsurpassed true Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, how could one bear to travel here with a body inherited from one's parents! In the past, Wang Zun climbed the nine-fold slopes and declared, "I am a loyal subject of the Han house." The Dharma Master, in traversing the snow-covered ridges to seek the scriptures, may also be called a true son of the Tathāgata.  Proceeding gradually, he reached the capital of Bāmīyāna, where there were more than ten monasteries and several thousand monks who studied the Lokottaravāda school (出世說部) of the Hīnayāna. The King of Bāmīyāna came out to welcome him and invited him into the palace to receive offerings; it was only after several days that he departed. There were two monks of the Mahāsāṃghika school (摩訶僧祇部), Āryadāsa (阿梨耶馱婆) and Āryasena (阿梨耶斯那), who were both deeply versed in the characteristics of the Dharma. Upon seeing the Dharma Master, they were astonished and exclaimed that such a monk could come from the distant land of China (脂那). They led him about to pay respects and observe the sites, showing him unceasing hospitality.

issues: Vārāṇasī (波剌拏斯國) → name genuinely uncertain: DM's (and Beal's: Bandras) reading kept, but the Xiyu ji has the bowl in Persia 波剌斯, of which 波剌拏斯 may be a corruption
en_revised: To the northeast of the royal city, there is a precious terrace where the Buddha’s bowl was once placed. The bowl later drifted and moved through various countries, and it is now present in the country of Vārāṇasī (波剌拏斯國; the Xiyu ji has Persia, 波剌斯). Eight or nine li to the southeast outside the city, there is a Pippala tree (畢鉢羅樹) over a hundred feet high; the four Buddhas of the past all sat beneath it, and there are now images of these four Tathāgatas there. The nine hundred and ninety-six Buddhas of the future will also sit there.
